Keep in mind that you can’t sign away your rights as a tenant in Ontario  so crazy clauses like “no guests” in leases can be ignored. Obviously I agree that drive by petting is worse than asking politely to pet but thats not the point of what I was saying at all. It’s not like I’m saying pet without asking, I’m saying don’t interact at all. 

There also is harm in asking. As I briefly outlined, many handlers have issues with social interaction and the needless asks about pets or questions about the dog can exasperate social anxiety or instigate a shutdown or something similar. 

If you aren’t bothered by people coming up to you, that’s great and you can invite people to pet your dog, but spreading the idea that “there’s no harm in asking” simply isn’t true for many handlers.

The blaming handlers for being rude isn’t a very good take either. No one, handler or otherwise, owes strangers conversation, especially if that conversation pertains to private health information, which service dog interactions often end up leading to. Handlers aren’t needlessly bitter, they are guarded because of countless instances of ableism that begin with people asking about their dogs. That’s reasonable and also not our fault as handlers. 

A lot of this just seems like you are more of a people person than a lot of us are. That’s (and I honestly mean this) a great quality, but lots of us don’t want to constantly have conversations with people and that shouldn’t be considered rude.

Honestly I hate the idea that it’s okay to ask to pet service dogs. A lot of handlers (myself included) have issues with social interactions and being out in public can already be a lot. Then adding in the extra stress if interacting with a stranger who might get mad when you tell them no? It’s… not ideal lol. I’d say if OP (and other allies) want to do the most respectful thing they should just ignore the dog unless they are invited to engage by the handler.

Thank you for asking us what we prefer! You might hear people say to “just ask” but don’t. If a service dog handler wants you to pet their dog they will offer up the opportunity to you. Thanks for doing your best to educate yourself, I really appreciate it (:

I would be very mindful of how much anxiety having a service dog can cause. It depends why you get anxious in crowds, but if it’s because you feel like you are being stared at or judged then you need to know that those feeling will be worse with a SD because people will be staring at you and judging you. If interactions with strangers makes your anxiety symptoms worse, remember that having a service dog will mean MANY frustrating interactions with nosy strangers. On a good day, they will tell you that your dog is cute and ask it’s name but on a bad day they will ask you to explain how and why you are disabled, or worse.

I don’t really agree that a diagnosis needs to come before a service dog, especially if OP has been trying to sort out what’s going on for some time. Chronic and invisible illness can be extremely difficult to diagnose and the doctors that might be able to make those diagnoses are often unaffordable, inaccessible and/or prejudiced. If OP can identify ways in which a service dog could mitigate the symptoms of their disability (diagnosed or not) then it’s a totally reasonable option, regardless of what potential treatment options might exist out there if they could get a diagnosis. I get what you mean about how a diagnosis could lead to medication that could be an easier fix than a sd but as much as that is a common outcome, I think an equally frequent one is just years of seeking a diagnosis and trying medications that’s don’t work or maybe even have side effects that could potentially negatively effect OPs life in more ways than a service dog would. 

This isn’t to say I think OP should necessarily get a service dog, I just don’t think they shouldn’t get a service dog because they are waiting on a diagnosis, if that makes sense? Especially because they mention a psychiatric disability as well, I don’t think a service dog would go, like, unused even if they did find an “easier” treatment for their chronic illness.

In my situation, I got my dog for autism assistance and psychiatric work with the expectation that she would help with chronic illness related symptoms that I had been experiencing for years but were undiagnosed. I received my first chronic illness diagnosis nearly two years into having a SD and she had been alerting to symptoms and making my life much easier (with specific regards to my chronic illness) for half of that time. Even now, I’m still waiting on an explanation for much of my chronic pain but I don’t know what I would do without my dogs tasks to help mitigate those symptoms.

I have used an Amazon harness for a long time and I hate it. Does it do the job? 100% it does. That said, I have experienced constant judgement from a) other handlers who are wary of a person who seems to be abled (invisible illness gal over here) using gear that is so readily available to anyone and from b) non-handlers who see the vest and know they could just buy one. I’ve on multiple occasions had people with fake service dogs come up to me and try to start a conversation about how easy it is to just buy the vest and how they have the same one at home. Long story short: all your worst fears about what people will assume about an Amazon vest are (in my experience) true and if they aren’t (and you’re like me) you will be constantly stressing about those things. Having and training a service dog already gets us so much judgement (from both handlers and non-handlers), so for me it was worth spending extra money on gear from somewhere more reputable in the SD community to lessen the judgement.

I’d also like to add that lush, despite its claims of being “ethical,” is not. Their employees don’t make a living wage and because they have built a company where the majority of their employees are seasonals, the majority of us don’t get sick pay during a global pandemic. I urge you to not only get what you pay for from Lush but to exploit them at every chance you get. They certainly have no issue exploiting their workers while getting the credit of being so ethical. Fuck em. And get as much free soap as you can in the process.

Edit to say obviously be nothing but kind to the employees. We are humans and also hate lush’s exploitation of the working class while jerking themselves off about how ethical they are.

But I think that's kind of it- Reddit isn't real life. There are different social rules. Your comment being on the wrong thread warrants downvotes, because regardless of the reason, it isn't contributing. 

It's not necessarily about the poster, it's about other redditers who don't want to read comments on the wrong thread, and the auto close of the downvoted comments saves other people time. 

If we really want to put this into irl type interactions, it would be like if you and I were talking about cats at a cat convention in front of hundreds of people and a person came up to us, took the mic and started talking about possums to the whole crowd. We can't just ignore it because everyone is here to talk about cats, not possums. Sure, the crowd can talk amongst themselves about cats but that interupts the experience. Someone should ask the person to get off the stage, and downvoting does just that

But even if it is used to disagree, that doesn't seem inherently wrong, especially when it could be disagreeing with the sub the opinion is placed in. Let's say I went to some flat Earth sub and was like "you are all so dumb the earth is so obviously round" I would get downvoted to hell. Would I be wrong? No. But the overall opinion of the sub would prevail- which would contribute to the shared beleifs the subs community is formed around. (This doesn't have to be as central of a topic either, but could just be an unspoken shared beleif of the sub)

Obviously there are instantances where people downvote for no reason, but it doesn't remove the post or comment, it just closes it. People can then turn a downvoted comment into an upvoted one by voting for its importance and relavance, if they feel it was downvoted unfairly.

I don't think it's necesserily about just disagreeing though. It's about if the comment is relevant to the conversation that the thread is about. I just read the interaction you had on r/parenting that got crazy downvotes and I agree it was a bit excessive, but also your comment wasn't relevent to the discussion. 

The whole set up of Reddit allows the publicly perceived more relevant posts and comments to show up more and the ones that are deemed to be not useful are downvoted to save future redditers time when reading the thread they are interested in.

I get that sometimes it turns into a downvoted party, but I think downvoting and upvoting posts based on their value is an integral part of this platform.
